passages.text: Introduction: Why Graphene Is Called a Wonder Material Graphene is one of the most talked-about materials in modern science. It is extremely thin, strong, lightweight, flexible, and highly conductive. Because of this unusual combination, researchers and industries are exploring graphene for electronics, batteries, coatings, composites, sensors, medical devices, water filtration, construction materials, textiles, and many other applications. In simple words, graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a flat honeycomb-like pattern. The Nobel Prize describes graphene as carbon atoms joined in a flat lattice similar to a honeycomb, but only one atom thick. It also notes that graphite contains millions of graphene layers stacked on top of one another. That is what makes graphene so interesting. Carbon is already familiar to us in forms such as graphite and diamond. But when carbon atoms are arranged as a single, flat layer, they behave in extraordinary ways. Graphene can conduct electricity and heat, bend without easily breaking, remain almost transparent in thin layers, and add strength to other materials. Discovery of Graphene Scientists had studied carbon materials for many years before graphene became famous. The big breakthrough came when researchers successfully isolated a stable single layer of graphene from graphite. Graphene was isolated in 2004 at the University of Manchester by Professor Andre Geim and Professor Kostya Novoselov. Their work later earned them the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics. The University of Manchester describes graphene as being discovered there in 2004 by Geim and Novoselov. The method was surprisingly simple. Britannica explains that Novoselov, Geim, and colleagues isolated single-layer graphene using exfoliation from graphite, often described as the “scotch-tape method.” This discovery opened the door to modern two-dimensional materials research. passages.text: What Is Graphene? Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms tightly arranged in a two-dimensional hexagonal honeycomb lattice. It is the foundational structural element of several other carbon allotropes, including graphite, carbon nanotubes, and fullerenes. Despite measuring only one atom in thickness—roughly 0.34 nanometers—graphene is one of the strongest, lightest, and most conductive materials known to modern science. The Core Definition and Structure of Graphene At an atomic level, graphene consists entirely of carbon atoms bound together through sp2 hybridization. In this configuration, each carbon atom shares strong covalent bonds with three adjacent neighbors in a planar sheet. The fourth valence electron occupies a vertical p-orbital, which delocalizes across the entire sheet to form overlapping pi bands. This delocalized electronic network gives graphene its extraordinary electrical and thermal conductivity. Because it comprises a single atomic layer, graphene is classified as a two-dimensional (2D) material. Prior to its physical isolation, theoretical physicists debated whether purely two-dimensional crystal lattices could remain thermodynamically stable at room temperature without curling, folding, or decomposing. Discovery and the Nobel Prize in Physics Carbon layers resembling graphene were observed in transmission electron microscopes for decades, but isolating a freestanding, single-atom-thick sheet remained elusive until 2004. This can improve electrical conductivity compared with graphene oxide, although it may not fully match pristine graphene. It is used in applications where a balance of processability and conductivity is needed, such as sensors, energy-storage materials, conductive coatings, and research devices. 5. They are commonly used as additives in plastics, rubber, coatings, lubricants, construction materials, composites, and thermal-management materials.
